blocks.x: Decision models wrapped in policy bounds, challenger benchmarks and explainable outputs: decisions a regulator can read, a panel can challenge, and a board can defend — with defer-to-human paths that are designed, not improvised.
A decision system is judged by its worst defensible case

Decision intelligence is where analytics stops advising and starts acting: credit lines, fraud holds, service credits, triage priorities. That step from report to action is governed differently — the decision needs a policy envelope, a challenger, an explanation shape and an appeal path before it earns the right to act.

We build the envelope first: what the decision may consider, what it may not, what it must explain, when it must defer to a human, and how its quality is measured against a signed benchmark panel. Only then does the model inside get tuned.
Below: the failure modes that make decision models indefensible, the reference architecture that wraps them in challenge and explanation, and the console the risk committee reads.
Four failure modes that make decisions indefensible
Each of these survives a demo and dies in a supervisory review — the countermeasures are the difference between a score and a decision.

blocks.caption: Decision Intelligence Systems: failure modes we design against — and the countermeasure that ships with the build
headers: What it looks like in production

Feature governance with proxy screening; disparate-impact tests per release
Score inflation

Time-based holdouts; champion-challenger on live traffic, not archives
Explanation theater
SHAP values that explain nothing a customer can act on
Reason-code taxonomy mapped to policy language; plain-language templates
Defer-to-human erosion
The model defers everything hard; humans become the fallback dump
Deferral budgets with quality-of-deferred metrics; deferral is scored too

blocks.x: Reference architecture — challenger panels around every decision

The architecture wraps the primary model in a challenger panel: agreement thresholds gate autonomy, disparate-impact monitors run continuously, and every output carries reason codes a human panel can audit line by line.

blocks.title: Reference architecture — governed decision service
blocks.note: The champion only acts inside the policy envelope; the challenger scores every case silently, and disagreement rates above threshold force a review before promotion.

widgets.title: Where each decision type sits — act fast vs explain deep

blocks.x: Decision stack defaults — and documented deviations
Defaults favor challenger coverage and reason-code completeness over raw accuracy; deviation triggers are written because each one has fairness or explainability consequences.

blocks.caption: Decision Intelligence Systems: default stack and the conditions under which we deviate
rows: Decision core
Gradient-boosted scorecards with rule overlays
Deep models only where the lift justifies the explanation cost
Challengers
Two permanent challengers scored silently on live traffic
Offline-only benchmarking — it misses population drift
Explanations
Reason-code taxonomy bound to policy language
Raw SHAP dumps as customer-facing explanations — unusable
Fairness
Disparate-impact and equal-opportunity tests per release
One-time fairness audit — drift makes it stale in months
Ledger
Immutable decision rows with envelope version
Logging only outcomes — inputs are what audits need
